..
Issued at 213 AM CST Sun Nov 1 2026

Scattered small clusters of convective showers and isolated 
thunderstorms were lifting across eastern portions of the 
forecast area early this morning. This weak convection was 
occurring in association with a sheared northwest-southeast area
of mid-level vorticity, coincident with a layer of steep lapse 
rates roughly in the 800-500 mb layer, as noted in current RAP 
soundings. Though model sounding ELs are just shy of -20C, MRMS 
isothermal reflectivity does indicate the tallest updrafts 
reaching the -20C level with some 40-45 dBZ cores. The 
expectation is that these scattered showers and isolated 
thunderstorms will continue to lift across far northeast IL and 
northwest IN (mainly east of the I-55 and I-355 corridors) prior
to sunrise before the sheared vort lobe moves northeast of the 
forecast area.

Another weak mid-level short wave was noted across the mid-
Missouri Valley early this morning, and is progged to track east
across the area later this morning and afternoon. The strongest
forcing and juxtaposition of the low-level baroclinic zone to 
our south suggests greater potential for measurable rain remains
largely south of our forecast area across central IL/IN, the 
presence of the mid-level trough, weak warm advection and 
reasonably moist profiles should support occasional spotty light
showers or sprinkles across the CWA during the day. Have 
maintained a 15-20% chance mention, highest generally 
along/south of I-80. Short-wave mid-level ridging is then 
indicated across the area tonight, in the wake of today's short 
wave passage. 

Attention then turns to our west, focused on the evolution and 
eastward progression of a complex long-wave upper trough and 
it's associated deep surface low. Guidance has come into better 
agreement with the upper trough axis (and embedded closed upper 
low) propagating east of the Rockies and onto the Plains late 
Monday, with a deepening sub-995 mb surface low developing into 
eastern South Dakota by early evening. This is forecast to 
induce strong southerly return flow into the Midwest within a 
tightening surface pressure gradient. For northern IL/IN, the 
main impacts Monday look to be the development of somewhat 
breezy southerly winds (though forecast soundings depict fairly 
shallow mixing, supporting gusts around 20 mph during the 
afternoon), the potential for low stratus to advect in from the 
southwest, and perhaps some scattered showers as isentropic 
ascent increases with an elevated warm frontal zone lifting 
across the area. While warmer temperatures are expected, the 
shallow mixing may limit this somewhat with forecast highs 
Monday are in the mid-upper 60s.

A strong mid-level short wave (currently off the northern Baja 
coast) is progged to wrap around the south/southeastern 
periphery of the larger scale upper trough late Monday/Monday 
night, further deepening the closed upper low over the Central 
Plains. This results in new surface low development (or 
redevelopment) southeastward across IA, eventually slowing as 
the system begins to become more vertically stacked on Tuesday. 
Forecast sounding and time/height sections indicate development 
of a ~45 kt low-level jet into the forecast area Monday night 
into Tuesday/Tuesday night ahead of the deepening system. 
Strengthening south winds will likely keep Monday night temps 
very mild with lows in the 55-60 degree range. Winds may gust in
excess of 30 mph during the day Tuesday, with temperatures 
potentially topping out in the low-mid 70s.

Deeper moisture feed during this process is initially focused 
west of the Mississippi River, due to the southwestern periphery
of high pressure ridging from the Gulf Coast to the mid-
Atlantic region. This moisture eventually looks to reach our 
area late Tuesday/Tuesday night however, with the greatest 
potential for showers and perhaps a few thunderstorms in this 
moisture axis ahead of the system's occluding cold front. The 
extent of thunderstorm coverage is a little uncertain, with 
models indicating a pinching off of the MUCAPE axis to the north
of the surface frontal occlusion Tuesday night. 

Confidence in forecast details then decreases mid-week, due to 
model differences in the further evolution of the slow-moving 
upper low across the region - complicated somewhat by the degree
of phasing with a northern stream short wave across the upper 
Midwest/northern Lakes. Overall, the Wednesday-Friday period 
continues to look unsettled as the closed upper low and occluded
surface system track slowly east across the region, though some
timing differences linger in the guidance at this distance. 
While no strong intrusion of colder air is evident at this time,
temperatures do look to eventually cool to/slightly below 
average on the back side of this departing system.

Ratzer
